name: Arturo Gatti
milestone_by_age_26: Won the IBF junior lightweight world championship on December 15, 1995 at age 23, defeating Tracy Harris Patterson at Madison Square Garden.
early_history_summary: Born in Cassino, Italy and raised in Montreal, Canada, Gatti entered a boxing gym at age seven, following his older brother Joe. He had a decorated amateur career with approximately 86-14 record, winning three Canadian Golden Gloves and two national junior championships. He turned professional at age 19 in 1991, relocating to Jersey City, New Jersey, and built a record of 17-0 before challenging for the world title.
family_context_summary: Born to Italian immigrant parents Giovanni and Ida Gatti; fourth of six children, raised in Montreal's Little Italy. Father passed away when Arturo was 15, motivating him to pursue boxing as a career.
parent_family_domain_summary: Older brother Joe Gatti was also a professional boxer, providing a direct family-domain pathway into the sport. Arturo followed Joe into boxing and into the same management circle.
primary_early_advantage_tags: brother boxer, early gym access, amateur reps, Gleason's Gym, father's death
evidence_summary: Arturo Gatti started boxing at age seven in Montreal, following his older brother Joe into the sport. After his father's death when he was 15, he committed to boxing professionally. He compiled an 86-14 amateur record with three Golden Gloves titles, turned pro at 19 in 1991, and won the IBF junior lightweight world title at age 23 in December 1995. His brother Joe's prior boxing career provided a direct family-domain pathway, and training at Gleason's Gym in Brooklyn immersed him in a high-level boxing ecosystem.
starting_point: Born in Cassino, Italy to Italian immigrant parents Giovanni and Ida Gatti; raised in Montreal's Little Italy as the fourth of six children in a working-class family. Father died when Arturo was 15.
current_position: Died on July 11, 2009 at age 37 in Porto de Galinhas, Brazil under controversial circumstances (officially ruled suicide). Final role: retired boxer (2007) and real estate worker in Montreal.

trajectory.event: Turned professional with a third-round knockout of Jose Gonzalez on June 10, 1991 in Secaucus, New Jersey.
Won the IBF junior lightweight world championship by defeating Tracy Harris Patterson at Madison Square Garden on December 15, 1995.
Defended his title against Wilson Rodriguez in a fight named Ring Magazine Fight of the Year.
Won the WBC super lightweight world championship, becoming a two-division world champion.
Announced retirement from professional boxing on July 14, 2007.
Died on July 11, 2009 in Brazil under controversial circumstances.
Inducted into the International Boxing Hall of Fame posthumously in his first year of eligibility.

name: Raimonds Pauls
milestone_by_age_26: Founded the Latvian Radio Light Music Sextet in 1956 at age 20 and recorded his first songs; received an award at the young composers' forum in Moscow in 1961 at age 25 for his cycle 'Portreti'.
early_history_summary: Born in 1936 in Riga, Latvia to a working-class family, Pauls began piano studies at age 4. He enrolled at the Emīls Dārziņš College of Music in 1946 and the Latvian State Conservatory in 1953, graduating in 1958. In 1956, while still a student, he co-founded the Latvian Radio Light Music Sextet and recorded his first songs, marking the beginning of his professional composing career.
family_context_summary: Born to a working-class family in Iļģuciems, Riga. Father Voldemārs was a glassblowing factory worker and grandfather Ādolfs also worked at the factory. Mother Alma was a seamstress. The family owned a goat and tended a small garden plot.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father played drums and grandfather played violin, which led to the decision to give young Raimonds a musical instrument. This family musical tradition directly catalyzed his early musical training.
primary_early_advantage_tags: conservatory training, radio platform, family musical tradition, early piano start
evidence_summary: Raimonds Pauls began piano at age 4, driven by a family musical tradition (father played drums, grandfather played violin). He entered the Emīls Dārziņš College of Music at age 10 and the Latvian State Conservatory at 17. At age 20 in 1956, he co-founded the Latvian Radio Light Music Sextet, recording his first songs and gaining a national radio platform. He received an award at the young composers' forum in Moscow in 1961 at age 25. His working-class background meant no financial safety net, but the conservatory pipeline and radio access provided institutional acceleration.
starting_point: Born in 1936 in Iļģuciems, Riga to a working-class family; father was a glassblowing factory worker and mother a seamstress, with a family tradition of amateur music (father played drums, grandfather played violin).
current_position: Retired but still active as Latvia's most distinguished composer; served as Latvia's Minister of Culture (1988-1993) and later as a Saeima deputy. Resides in Riga, Latvia.

trajectory.event: Co-founded the Latvian Radio Light Music Sextet and recorded his first songs, launching his professional composing career.
Graduated from the Latvian State Conservatory with a concert pianist's diploma and joined the Latvian Philharmonia.
Received an award at the young composers' forum in Moscow for his cycle 'Portreti' (Portraits).
Became musical director, conductor, and pianist of the Riga Light Music Orchestra.
Composed 'Dāvāja Māriņa meitenei mūžiņu,' which became 'A Million Scarlet Roses' when covered by Alla Pugacheva, an international hit.
Named People's Artist of the USSR, the highest artistic honor in the Soviet Union.
Appointed Minister of Culture of Latvia, serving until 1993.

name: Richard Wagner
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found; called to the Quebec Bar in 1980 at age 23 and practiced law, but his judicial appointments (Superior Court 2004, Supreme Court 2012, Chief Justice 2017) all came well after age 26.

family_context_summary: Born to a prominent legal and political family in Montreal. Father Claude Wagner was a lawyer, crown attorney, judge, Quebec's minister of justice, MP, and senator. Mother was Gisèle Normandeau.

evidence_summary: Richard Wagner was called to the Quebec Bar in 1980 at age 23 and practiced commercial litigation at Lavery, de Billy. name: Dolph Lundgren
milestone_by_age_26: Won the European Kyokushin Karate Heavyweight Championship in 1980 at age 23 and retained the title in 1981; also won the Australian Kyokushinkai Full-Contact Karate Tournament in 1982.
early_history_summary: Born in Stockholm, Sweden in 1957, Lundgren began judo at 16 and switched to Kyokushin karate shortly after. He trained under Sensei Brian Fitkin and competed in the 1979 World Open Karate Tournament in Tokyo as a green belt. He won the European heavyweight championship in 1980 and 1981, earned his black belt in 1981, and simultaneously pursued chemical engineering, completing his master's at the University of Sydney in 1982.
family_context_summary: Born to an academic middle-class family in Stockholm. Father Karl Hugo Johan Lundgren was an engineer (M.Sc.) and economist for the Swedish government; mother Sigrid Birgitta was a language teacher. Father was physically abusive, which Lundgren said motivated his ambition. Elder brother Johan was also an engineer.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father and elder brother were both engineers, creating an academic family environment. Father's abusive behavior created adversity that Lundgren channeled into competitive drive. No direct martial arts family domain.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Sensei Brian Fitkin, Kyokushin training, academic scholarships, adversity from abusive father, physical size
evidence_summary: Dolph Lundgren began martial arts at 16 in Sweden, training under Sensei Brian Fitkin in Kyokushin karate. He competed at the 1979 World Open Tournament in Tokyo as a green belt, then won the European heavyweight championship in 1980 and 1981 at ages 23-24. He simultaneously pursued chemical engineering on academic scholarships, earning his master's from the University of Sydney in 1982. His father was an engineer for the Swedish government but was physically abusive, creating adversity that fueled Lundgren's competitive drive. His Fulbright scholarship to MIT in 1983 led him to New York and eventually acting.
starting_point: Born in Stockholm, Sweden to an academic middle-class family; father was an engineer and economist for the Swedish government, mother a language teacher. Father was physically abusive, which motivated Lundgren's ambition.
current_position: Active actor and filmmaker; became a US citizen in 2024. Married Emma Krokdal in 2023. Resides in Los Angeles. Net worth estimated at approximately $18 million.

Won the European Kyokushin Karate Heavyweight Championship, establishing himself as a top full-contact karate competitor.

Breakthrough film role as Ivan Drago in Rocky IV, launching his international acting career.
Reprised the role of Ivan Drago in Creed II, returning to the character that made him famous.

name: Jan Janssen
milestone_by_age_26: Won the 1964 World Professional Road Race Championship at age 24, along with Paris-Nice and the Tour de France points classification in the same year; also won Tour de France stages in 1963 at age 23.
early_history_summary: Born in Nootdorp, Netherlands in 1940, Janssen joined the cycling club at Delft at age 16 and won 25 races as a novice in two years. He had a successful amateur career winning several Dutch classics and rode the Tour de l'Avenir for the Netherlands. He turned professional in 1962 at age 22 with Pelforth-Sauvage-Lejeune and quickly became one of the top sprinters in the peloton.
family_context_summary: Born in Nootdorp, a small town near The Hague. Worked with his parents as a youth in the family construction firm, digging foundations. Later moved to Putte, a village on the Belgian border.
parent_family_domain_summary: Family ran a construction firm; no direct cycling domain background documented. The physical labor of excavating foundations may have contributed to physical conditioning.
primary_early_advantage_tags: cycling club at 16, 25 novice wins, Dutch cycling culture, physical labor background
evidence_summary: Jan Janssen joined the cycling club at Delft at age 16 and won 25 races as a novice in two years, demonstrating exceptional early talent. He turned professional in 1962 at age 22 and won his first Tour de France stage in 1963 at age 23. In 1964 at age 24, he won the World Professional Road Race Championship, Paris-Nice, and the Tour de France points classification. His working-class family background in construction provided no financial platform but the Dutch cycling culture and his early club participation gave him a strong start.
starting_point: Born in Nootdorp, Netherlands just days after the Dutch surrender to the Nazis; raised in a working-class family that ran a small construction firm, where Jan worked digging foundations as a youth.
current_position: Retired; living in Putte, Netherlands. As of 2023, he is the oldest surviving winner of the Tour de France.

trajectory.event: Turned professional with Pelforth-Sauvage-Lejeune after a successful amateur career.
Won his first Tour de France stage, establishing himself as a top sprinter in the professional peloton.
Won the World Professional Road Race Championship in Sallanches, Paris-Nice, and the Tour de France points classification.
Won the Vuelta a España and Paris-Roubaix, cementing his status as one of cycling's greats.
Won the Tour de France, becoming the first Dutch rider to do so, by just 38 seconds.
Retired from professional cycling after 11 seasons.

name: Daniel Day-Lewis
milestone_by_age_26: Took over the lead role in the West End play 'Another Country' in late 1982 at age 25, and appeared in the film 'Gandhi' (1982); joined the Royal Shakespeare Company in 1983 at age 26, playing Romeo in Romeo and Juliet.
early_history_summary: Born in London in 1957, Day-Lewis made his film debut at 14 in Sunday Bloody Sunday (1971). He trained at the Bristol Old Vic Theatre School for three years, performing in Bristol theatre productions through the early 1980s. He had his big theatre break in late 1982 taking over the lead in 'Another Country,' appeared in Gandhi (1982), and joined the RSC in 1983 playing Romeo.
family_context_summary: Born into a prominent literary and artistic family. Father Cecil Day-Lewis was Poet Laureate of the United Kingdom. Mother Jill Balcon was an actress. Grandfather Sir Michael Balcon was head of Ealing Studios, a founding figure of British cinema. Sister Tamasin is a food critic and filmmaker.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was Poet Laureate; mother was a professional actress; maternal grandfather was head of Ealing Studios. This is an exceptionally strong family-domain advantage in literature, theatre, and film, providing direct industry fluency and networks from birth.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Poet Laureate father, actress mother, Ealing Studios grandfather, Bristol Old Vic, RSC, London arts elite
evidence_summary: Daniel Day-Lewis was born into one of Britain's most distinguished artistic families: his father was Poet Laureate Cecil Day-Lewis, his mother was actress Jill Balcon, and his grandfather Sir Michael Balcon headed Ealing Studios. He made his film debut at 14, trained at the Bristol Old Vic Theatre School, and performed in Bristol theatre productions through the early 1980s. His big theatre break came in late 1982 at age 25 taking over the lead in 'Another Country,' followed by a small role in Gandhi (1982) and joining the Royal Shakespeare Company in 1983 as Romeo. The family-domain advantage in literature, theatre, and film was exceptionally strong and directly catalytic.
starting_point: Born in Kensington, London into one of Britain's most prominent artistic families: father Cecil Day-Lewis was Poet Laureate, mother Jill Balcon was an actress, and grandfather Sir Michael Balcon was head of Ealing Studios.
current_position: Retired from acting in 2017 (announced); knighted in 2014. Returning to screen for film 'Anemone' directed by his son Ronan. Resides in Ireland. Net worth estimated at approximately $60 million.

Had his big theatre break taking over the lead in 'Another Country' in London's West End and appeared in a small role in the film Gandhi.
Joined the Royal Shakespeare Company, playing Romeo in Romeo and Juliet and Flute in A Midsummer Night's Dream on a national tour.
Breakthrough film performances in My Beautiful Laundrette and A Room with a View, both released to critical acclaim.
Won the Academy Award for Best Actor for My Left Foot, his first Oscar.
Won his third Academy Award for Best Actor for Lincoln, becoming the first male actor to win three Best Actor Oscars.
Knighted by Queen Elizabeth II for services to drama.

name: Olivia Newton-John
milestone_by_age_26: Released her first solo album 'If Not for You' in 1971 at age 23, with the title track becoming her first international hit; became a regular on BBC TV's 'It's Cliff Richard' giving her massive UK exposure.
early_history_summary: Born in Cambridge, England in 1948, Newton-John moved to Australia at age 6. She formed a folk group at 14, won a TV talent contest at 17, and moved to England in 1966 where she recorded her first single. She formed a duo with Pat Carroll, performed on TV shows, and was selected for the manufactured group Toomorrow before releasing her breakthrough solo album in 1971.
family_context_summary: Born into a highly academic family. Grandfather Max Born was a Nobel Prize-winning physicist and one of the founders of quantum mechanics. Father Brinley Newton-John was an MI5 officer during WWII and later a university professor. Mother Irene Born was the daughter of Max Born. Parents divorced when Olivia was 10.
parent_family_domain_summary: No direct music industry family background. Father was an academic and former intelligence officer. However, the family's intellectual and cultural milieu, plus the father's aspirations as an opera singer, provided a culturally rich environment. Grandfather Max Born's academic eminence provided social connections.
primary_early_advantage_tags: TV talent show, Australian TV exposure, BBC Cliff Richard show, Pat Carroll duo, academic family
evidence_summary: Olivia Newton-John grew up in an academic family (grandfather Max Born won the Nobel Prize in Physics) in Australia after moving from England at age 6. She began performing at 14, won a TV talent contest at 17, and moved to England in 1966 at age 18. After early struggles with her debut single, she built a career through TV appearances and a duo with Pat Carroll, leading to her first solo album 'If Not for You' in 1971 at age 23, which produced her first international hit. Her parents' divorce at age 10 created adversity, and her father's academic career provided a middle-class but not wealthy platform.
starting_point: Born in Cambridge, England to an academic family; grandfather Max Born was a Nobel Prize-winning physicist, father Brinley Newton-John was an MI5 officer and university professor. Family moved to Australia when Olivia was 6; parents divorced when she was 10.
current_position: Died on August 8, 2022 at age 73 in Santa Ynez, California, after a long battle with breast cancer. Final role: singer, actress, and breast cancer research advocate.

trajectory.event: Won the Australian TV talent contest Sing, Sing, Sing, earning a trip to England that launched her professional music career.
Recorded her first single 'Till You Say You'll Be Mine' for Decca Records in Britain and began performing on the UK club circuit.
Released her first solo album 'If Not for You,' with the title track becoming her first international hit.
Represented the UK in the Eurovision Song Contest, placing 4th, and had her first US No. 1 single with 'I Honestly Love You.'},{

event.name: Shaquille O'Neal
event.milestone_by_age_26: Named AP Player of the Year and First-team All-American as a sophomore at LSU in 1990-91 at age 18-19; selected as the #1 overall pick in the 1992 NBA draft at age 20; won NBA Rookie of the Year in 1992-93 at age 20-21.
event.early_history_summary: Born in Newark, New Jersey in 1972, O'Neal was raised by his mother Lucille and stepfather Phillip Harrison, a career Army sergeant. The family moved to military bases in Germany and Texas. At 6'9" as a high school junior, he dominated at Robert G. Cole High School in San Antonio. He enrolled at LSU in 1989 at age 17, where coach Dale Brown had identified him years earlier in Germany. As a sophomore in 1990-91, he averaged 27.6 points and was named AP Player of the Year.
event.family_context_summary: Born to teenage mother Lucille O'Neal and biological father Joe Toney, who was imprisoned for drug possession when Shaq was an infant. Stepfather Phillip Harrison, a career Army sergeant, raised Shaq from age 2 and provided strict discipline and guidance. Family moved frequently due to military postings.
event.parent_family_domain_summary: Biological father Joe Toney played high school basketball (All-State guard) and was offered a scholarship to Seton Hall, indicating genetic athletic advantage. Stepfather Phillip Harrison provided military discipline and encouraged Shaq's basketball career. No direct professional basketball family background.
event.primary_early_advantage_tags: exceptional height and size, LSU coach Dale Brown, military discipline, Boys & Girls Clubs, AP Player of the Year
event.evidence_summary: Shaquille O'Neal's extraordinary physical size (6'9" as a high school junior, eventually 7'1") was the dominant early advantage, changing institutional response at every level. His biological father was an All-State high school basketball guard, suggesting genetic athletic inheritance. Stepfather Phillip Harrison, a career Army sergeant, provided strict discipline and relocated the family to military bases. LSU coach Dale Brown identified O'Neal at age 13 in Germany and recruited him to LSU, where O'Neal was named AP Player of the Year as a sophomore at age 18-19. The Boys & Girls Clubs provided early gym access in Newark. No financial safety net existed, but the physical prodigy edge was exceptional and directly catalytic.
event.starting_point: Born in Newark, New Jersey to a teenage mother and a biological father who was imprisoned for drug possession; raised by stepfather Phillip Harrison, a career Army sergeant, in a military family that moved frequently. Working-class background with no financial safety net.
event.current_position: Retired from NBA in 2011; works as a sports analyst on TNT's Inside the NBA. Net worth estimated at approximately $400-500 million. Resides in the United States.

trajectory.event: Enrolled at Louisiana State University (LSU) and began his college basketball career under coach Dale Brown.
Named AP Player of the Year and First-team All-American as a sophomore at LSU, averaging 27.6 points per game.
Selected as the #1 overall pick in the 1992 NBA draft by the Orlando Magic.
Named NBA Rookie of the Year after averaging 23.4 points and 13.9 rebounds in his debut season.
Won his first NBA championship with the Los Angeles Lakers and was named NBA Finals MVP.
Won his second consecutive NBA championship with the Lakers and was named NBA Finals MVP again.
Won his fourth NBA championship with the Miami Heat.
Retired from professional basketball after a 19-year NBA career.
